title: The Robot with Hiccups
description: Nia built a tower of blocks.
pages: Nia built a tower of blocks. Her robot, Beep, brought the last block. “Thank you,” Nia said. “HIC!” said Beep.
The block jumped out of his hand. It landed on the rug. Beep looked at Nia. “That was new,” he said.
Nia asked Beep to stand still. HIC! A little door on his back popped open. Something round fell out.
It was a marble. Nia had lost it while they were playing. “You are not a marble box,” she told Beep.
Nia called Dad. He switched Beep off before checking the open door. A second marble was stuck inside. Dad took it out.
Dad closed the door and switched Beep on. Beep picked up the block. This time, his hand stayed still. The tower was safe.
Nia put both marbles in a jar. She drew a marble on its lid. “These go here,” she said. Beep nodded.
Beep set the last block on top. “Ta-da!” he said. Nia jumped. “Not another hiccup!” “No,” said Beep. “That was on purpose.”

title: The Runaway Sandwich
description: Ben took a wrapped sandwich to the park.
pages: Ben took a wrapped sandwich to the park. He set it on the picnic blanket. His dog, Pip, lay beside him.
A gust of wind lifted one corner of the blanket. The sandwich rolled down the grassy hill. “My lunch!” Ben cried.
Pip ran after it. Ben ran after Pip. The sandwich bumped over a root and stopped beside a bench.
Pip reached it first. He sniffed the paper. Ben held his breath. “Leave it, Pip,” he said. Pip sat down.
Ben picked up the sandwich. The wrapper was muddy and torn. He took it back to Mom. “It had quite a trip.”
Mom put the ruined sandwich in the trash. She had extra bread and cheese in their picnic bag. Ben helped make a fresh lunch.
They moved to a flat spot. Ben put his plate on the table. Pip lay under it and got his own dog treat.
Ben took a bite. Nothing rolled away. “Good sandwich,” he said. Pip thumped his tail. Ben added, “Good dog, too.”

title: A Dragon at the Library
description: Luz found a tiny dragon on the library steps.
pages: Luz found a tiny dragon on the library steps. It had purple wings and a very sad face. “I lost my story,” it said.
“Was it in a book?” Luz asked. The dragon nodded. “A big tree. A small door. A pie.” That was all it remembered.
Luz took the dragon to the librarian. “We need a tree and a pie,” she said. The librarian smiled. “Let us look.”
The first book had a tree, but no pie. The second had a pie, but no door. The dragon shook its head.
The third book had a mouse who lived in a tree. On the cover, the mouse carried a pie through a small door.
“That is it!” cried the dragon. A puff of smoke curled from its nose. “Indoor voice,” Luz whispered. “Sorry,” said the dragon.
Luz read beside the dragon. At the funny part, they both giggled softly. The dragon tucked its wings close to make room.
When the library closed, the dragon borrowed the book. “Now I have my story,” it said. Luz waved. “And a library card!”

title: Turtle Taxi
description: Turtle sat beside a wide puddle.
pages: Turtle sat beside a wide puddle. Mouse stood on the other side. “My feet will get wet,” Mouse called. “Hop on,” said Turtle.
Mouse stepped onto Turtle’s shell. Turtle walked slowly through the shallow water. Mouse kept his tail curled up. “A taxi!” Mouse said.
At the far edge, Mouse hopped off. “Thank you.” Turtle liked helping. He put a leaf beside the puddle to mark his taxi stop.
Beetle came next. She was easy to carry. Then Rabbit arrived. Turtle looked at Rabbit. Rabbit looked at Turtle. “Too big,” they both said.
Rabbit found a narrow part of the puddle. One hop took him across. He waved back. Turtle waved one short leg.
A breeze pushed Mouse’s empty basket into the water. It floated toward Turtle. Mouse called, “Can your taxi carry a basket?”
Turtle nudged it gently to the bank. Mouse caught the handle. There was no mouse on this trip, but the taxi still helped.
By evening, the puddle was smaller. Mouse could step over it. Turtle took down his leaf. “Taxi closed,” he said. “Time for lettuce.”

title: The Missing Train Whistle
description: Ellis took his wooden whistle to the park railway.
pages: Ellis took his wooden whistle to the park railway. He blew one soft toot. The driver waved from the little green engine.
Ellis put the whistle in his coat pocket. Then he and Dad sat in an open car. The train rolled past ducks and tall reeds.
At the next stop, Ellis reached for his whistle. His pocket was empty. He checked the seat. No whistle. “It is gone!”
Dad helped him look in the car. They stayed away from the track. The driver said, “We can ask at the station when we return.”
Ellis tried to remember. He had put the whistle away before sitting down. Then he had taken off his coat because the sun felt warm.
“My coat!” he said. It was folded beside Dad. Ellis had checked the pocket in his pants. He had forgotten about the coat.
He reached into the coat pocket. There was the whistle. “Found it!” Dad grinned. “It rode the whole way with us.”
Back at the station, Ellis gave one soft toot. The engine answered with its own whistle. “Yours is louder,” Ellis told the driver. “Mine fits in a pocket.”

title: The Caboose Club
description: Ruby had a club with two members: herself and her brother, Kit.
pages: Ruby had a club with two members: herself and her brother, Kit. Their meetings took place under the kitchen table. They needed a better clubhouse. Kit kept bumping his head whenever he voted.
At the railway museum, Ruby spotted a red caboose. Long ago, a caboose rode at the back of a freight train. This one stood on a short piece of track with flowers around its wheels.

Mr. Park, the guide, let them climb inside. There were benches, cupboards, and a little desk. “A perfect clubhouse,” Ruby whispered. On the desk sat a locked tin box. Something rattled when Mr. Park lifted it.

“We found this during the repairs,” he said. “The key is missing.” Kit imagined gold coins. Ruby guessed train tickets. Mr. Park said they could help look through the museum’s old photographs for clues.
One photograph showed a railway worker sitting at the desk. A small key hung from a hook above his shoulder. Ruby pointed. “Was there a hook in the caboose?” Mr. Park took them back to check.
The hook was empty. Under it, Kit noticed a narrow gap behind the desk. Mr. Park shone a flashlight into the gap. A rusty key lay at the bottom. He used a long tool to reach it.
The key turned with a click. Inside the box were buttons, a pencil stub, and a folded paper. Kit sighed at the missing gold. Ruby unfolded the paper. It was a drawing of the caboose, made by a child.
On the back, someone had written, For Dad, so you can have a picture of home at work. The drawing showed a tiny house in every window. Ruby smiled. “They put home inside the train.”
Mr. Park made a copy for visitors to see and kept the old paper safe. He invited the children to help at the next family day. They could show other children how to draw their own caboose.
Ruby added a third member to the club: Mr. Park. They met at a museum table, where nobody bumped their head. Kit drew a caboose filled with gold coins. “This one,” he said, “is just pretend.”

title: The Snake Who Missed the Parade
description: Sedge the snake had practiced waving for the forest parade.
pages: Sedge the snake had practiced waving for the forest parade. Waving was difficult without arms. He tried his tail, but every time he raised it, he rolled sideways into a fern. His paper crown fell off twice.

On parade morning, Rabbit brought him a ribbon. “Tie this to your tail,” she said. “Then everyone can see you wave.” Sedge tried it. The ribbon fluttered beautifully. He was ready—except for one small problem.
The parade started at the big oak. Sedge went to the big elm. He waited beside a beetle, who was not in the parade. “Quiet crowd,” Sedge said. Far away, he heard a drum.
He followed the sound to the oak. Only an empty lemonade jug remained. The parade had already left. Sedge’s crown drooped. He could see the last bright ribbons disappearing around a bend in the path.

Then the drum stopped. Sedge hurried around the bend. A branch had fallen across the narrow path. The animals were arguing. Rabbit could hop over, but the little hedgehogs could not pull their flower cart across.
Sedge slipped under the branch to see the other side. Just beyond it, a wide garden gate stood open. Through the gate was a smooth path that joined the parade road farther ahead.
“Come this way!” he called. Nobody heard him over the argument. Sedge raised his ribbon and shook it. This time, Rabbit spotted the bright flash. “Sedge has found something!” she said.
He led them back a few steps and through the gate. The cart rolled easily along the garden path. The smallest hedgehog offered Sedge a place on top, beside a pot of daisies.
Sedge rode through the village with his ribbon waving high. He did not have to lift his tail, balance his crown, and move all at once. The beetle from the elm flew over to watch.
“You found your parade,” said the beetle. Sedge nodded. “Eventually.” Then his crown tipped over one eye. Rabbit straightened it, the drum began again, and the flower cart rattled toward the picnic.

title: The Pancake Planet
description: On a tiny moon, Tavi ran the only pancake café for a hundred space miles.
pages: On a tiny moon, Tavi ran the only pancake café for a hundred space miles. Her helper was a round robot named Dot. Dot could flip six pancakes at once, but he always called them flat circles.

One morning, a delivery ship landed with a new cooker. The old one had broken. Tavi followed the setup pictures while Dot arranged plates. Outside, hungry travelers began lining up in their shiny space boots.

Tavi poured the first pancake. She pressed a green button. The pancake rose from the cooker and floated toward the ceiling. “That,” said Dot, “is not where the plate is.” A second pancake floated after it.
Tavi shut off the cooker. The pancakes drifted gently down. Dot caught one on a plate and the other on his head. Tavi read the button label: FLOAT MODE. The cooker was made for space kitchens.

There was another button marked PAN MODE. Tavi pressed it. This pancake stayed where it belonged. Dot flipped it neatly. The travelers cheered through the café window. Breakfast was saved—or so Tavi thought.
Then the syrup bottle would not open. Dot twisted. Tavi twisted. Nothing happened. The first traveler tapped on the window. He pointed at a picture on his own bottle and made a pushing motion.

Tavi looked closely at the cap. A tiny arrow pointed down. She pushed and turned. The cap opened. “Two things to do together,” she told Dot. “Not one thing to do harder.” Dot wiped syrup from his fingers.
Soon every plate had a warm pancake. One traveler asked about the pancake on Dot’s head. Dot had forgotten it. “My new hat,” he said. Tavi removed it before it could slide into his open tool box.
After breakfast, they made a small sign for each button. Tavi drew a pan beside PAN MODE. Dot drew a pancake near the ceiling beside FLOAT MODE. He added a very surprised robot underneath it.
That afternoon, a new ship arrived. “Do you serve flying pancakes?” the pilot asked. Tavi looked at Dot. Dot looked at the cooker. “Only by accident,” Tavi said, and brought out two ordinary plates.

title: The Library Under the Stairs
description: At the community center, Hana waited while her dad helped paint a wall.
pages: At the community center, Hana waited while her dad helped paint a wall. She had finished her book twice. Her friend Mo had finished his snack. Neither wanted to watch paint dry for another minute.
Mo noticed a narrow door under the stairs. A sign said STORAGE. They asked the center manager, Mrs. Reed, what was inside. “Mostly boxes,” she said. “You may look with me, but it is dusty.”
Behind the door stood three shelves full of books. Some had worn covers. Others looked nearly new. A little chair was buried under a pile of coats. Hana brushed dust from a book about sea monsters.
“These came from the old reading room,” Mrs. Reed said. “We never found a place for them.” Hana looked around. The space was small, but the chair fit. “What if the place is right here?”

Mrs. Reed measured the doorway and checked the light. Adults moved the heavy boxes. Hana and Mo wiped the shelves. Under the coats they found a second chair—and a cat, who had been asleep on the first.

The cat belonged to the caretaker. He took her to a quieter room. The children sorted books into picture books, stories, and books about real things. Mo wanted a shelf just for sea monsters. Hana said one book was not enough.
They made a sign for the new reading nook. Hana wrote in tiny, neat letters. From the hallway, nobody could read it. Mo tried letters as big as his hand. Now the sign could be seen from the door.
On opening day, a little girl stopped outside. “Can I come in?” she asked. Hana moved her chair to make room. The girl picked the sea-monster book. Mo grinned. His special shelf had its first reader.
Soon the nook was full, so Mrs. Reed put a basket of books and two more chairs in the hall. Children could choose a book inside and read where there was space. Nobody had to wait for a seat.

Dad finished painting. “Ready to go?” he asked. Hana held up one finger. She was nearly at the end of a chapter. Mo was reading about whales. Even without a sea-monster shelf, the little library was doing very well.

title: The Dinosaur on the Wrong Bus
description: Tobin the dinosaur was going to his cousin’s birthday party.
pages: Tobin the dinosaur was going to his cousin’s birthday party. He wore his best blue backpack. Inside was a gift wrapped in orange paper. On his wrist, Dad had written the bus number: 6.
At the busy station, Tobin saw a bus with a round number on the front. He hurried aboard. He found a seat beside a turtle carrying flowers. “Lovely day for the park,” the turtle said.
“I am going to a party,” Tobin replied. Then he looked out. The bus turned away from his cousin’s street. A sign inside said ROUTE 9. Tobin looked at his wrist. His stomach gave a small flip.
He stayed in his seat until the next stop. Then he told the driver, “I think I am on the wrong bus.” The driver parked safely before answering. “We will help you get to the right place.”

The driver called the station helper. At the next station, a helper in a bright vest met Tobin and phoned Dad. Tobin felt much better when he heard Dad’s voice. “Stay with the helper,” Dad said. “I am coming.”
While they waited, Tobin looked at the number on his wrist. With his arm held one way, the 6 looked like a 9. The helper showed him the printed route number and the list of stops on the wall.
Dad arrived with a new plan. They would ride together on bus 6. Tobin checked the number on the front, then checked the stops. His cousin’s street was on the list. This time, he was sure.
They reached the party after the first game, but before the cake. Tobin gave his cousin the orange package. Inside was a toy bus. His cousin rolled it across the table. “Where does this one go?”

“Anywhere you want,” Tobin said. “But check the number first.” He told the story while everyone ate cake. The turtle from the bus appeared at the garden gate. She was delivering flowers to Tobin’s aunt.
“You found your party!” she said. Tobin nodded and offered her a slice of cake. The toy bus carried one tiny paper flag across the table. Its number was 6, with a line underneath.

title: The Train That Carried a Garden
description: The village flower show was tomorrow, and Mr.
pages: The village flower show was tomorrow, and Mr. Vale had a problem. His delivery van had broken down beside the greenhouse. Forty pots of flowers stood ready to travel. “Perhaps they can walk,” said his niece, Imogen. Mr. Vale did not laugh.

The show was in a town served by the old valley railway. Imogen remembered a wagon at the station that carried bicycles. She asked whether it could carry flowers instead. Her uncle called the railway manager, who agreed to inspect the load.

The manager measured the pots and checked the wagon’s limits. Heavy pots would sit low, with straps around their stands. Smaller pots would travel in crates. Nobody would ride with the plants. “Flowers need tickets too?” Imogen asked. “Freight paperwork,” the manager replied.

Loading took much longer than Imogen expected. A tall sunflower brushed the doorway of the goods shed. Her friend Arun suggested laying it flat, but Mr. Vale shook his head. The stem might bend. They needed a lower stand, not a shorter flower.

Arun found a shallow crate. The sunflower’s pot fitted snugly inside. Once the crate was secured, the flower stood below the shed doorway. Imogen tied a small blue tag to each pot so the unloading crew would know which plants belonged together.

The train departed in the morning. Imogen and Arun rode in a passenger carriage with Mr. Vale. At every bend, Imogen tried to see the flower wagon. She could glimpse yellow blossoms behind the engine. It looked as if the railway had grown petals.

Halfway to town, the train stopped at a signal. They waited. Then the guard walked through the carriage: a fallen tree was blocking the line ahead. A railway crew was clearing it, but nobody knew exactly how long that would take.

Mr. Vale checked his watch. Entries closed at noon. If they missed the deadline, the flowers could still be displayed, but they could not win a prize. Imogen had spent weeks helping grow them. She stared at the unmoving hills and said nothing.

Arun opened his sketchbook. He drew the flower wagon waiting beside a field of sheep. One sheep in the drawing wore a sunflower hat. Imogen laughed despite herself. She added an engine with leaves instead of smoke. Soon they were designing an entire garden railway.

The train finally moved, but they reached town after noon. Mr. Vale spoke to the show organizer. The deadline applied to everyone. He nodded, disappointed, and accepted a display space near the entrance. Together they arranged their late garden around Arun’s drawing.

Visitors stopped to ask about the picture. Imogen told them about the broken van, the low crate, and the fallen tree. Children searched the drawing for the sheep in the hat. By afternoon, the entrance had become the busiest corner of the show.

Their flowers won no ribbon. On the journey home, however, Imogen carried a stack of requests for next year’s garden railway display. Mr. Vale finally laughed at her walking-flower joke. “They have traveled by train,” he said. “They will expect first class next time.”

title: Operation Invisible Hamster
description: The class hamster was called Professor Crumb, although he had never written a paper or taught a lesson.
pages: The class hamster was called Professor Crumb, although he had never written a paper or taught a lesson. On Friday, his empty cage caused more excitement than any teacher. The small door stood open. A sunflower seed rested on the desk beneath it.

Ms. Ortiz closed the classroom door and asked everyone to stand still. “We need a quiet search,” she said. “No grabbing, and no moving heavy furniture yourselves.” Maya wrote PROFESSOR CRUMB: MISSING on the board. Owen drew a hamster with a detective hat.

They checked the door’s clip. It had not clicked fully shut after the hamster’s water was changed. Ms. Ortiz secured the empty cage, then assigned search areas. Maya and Owen could inspect the reading corner without moving the large bookcase.

Owen found a crumb beside a floor cushion. “Evidence!” he whispered. Maya looked at it. It was pink. Professor Crumb’s food was brown. “That might be from yesterday’s party,” she said. Owen crossed out CRUMB OF GREAT IMPORTANCE in his notebook.

A rustle came from the art cupboard. Everyone froze. Ms. Ortiz opened it slowly. A roll of paper slid forward, followed by three paintbrushes. No hamster. “He is invisible,” Owen announced. “Or we have not found him,” Maya replied.

Maya studied the room from floor level. Behind the reading cushions, a cardboard tube led into the class’s model town. The town had streets, shops, and a railway station made from a cereal box. A sunflower seed lay just inside the tube.

The station roof was removable. Ms. Ortiz lifted it carefully. Professor Crumb sat in the ticket office, washing his face. He had packed the room with shredded paper. The class gave a silent cheer, waving their hands instead of shouting.

Ms. Ortiz used his familiar carrier to move him safely back to the cage. Owen wanted to know how long he had lived at the station. Maya pointed out that finding one seed could not tell them when he had arrived.

They repaired the cage clip and added a picture checklist beside it: door, clip, water. Two people would check the door after each supervised care session. Professor Crumb immediately began rearranging his bedding, apparently dissatisfied with his official home.

The cardboard station was not so easy to repair. One corner had been chewed into a round arch. Owen said it looked better that way. Maya added a tiny sign: HAMSTER ENTRANCE. Ms. Ortiz kept the model safely away from the cage.

For their class news, Maya wrote what they had observed. Owen wanted to include the invisible-hamster theory. She let him add it under a heading called Our First Guesses. Under What We Found, they described the tube and the seed.

On Monday, visitors admired the model town. Owen showed them the hamster entrance and the detective notebook. Professor Crumb slept through the whole presentation. “Secret agents need rest,” Owen whispered. Maya did not argue. It was a much better story when labeled pretend.

title: The Storm in the Museum
description: Leo’s favorite museum exhibit was a model ship inside a glass case.
pages: Leo’s favorite museum exhibit was a model ship inside a glass case. Each Saturday, a projector made waves ripple behind it, and speakers played a storm. This Saturday, Leo’s cousin Amara came to see it. Leo promised her the biggest indoor thunder in town.

They pressed the blue button. Lights flashed. Wind howled. Then a tiny squeak sounded from the speaker. The waves stopped. A recorded voice announced, “Please enjoy the magnificent squeak.” Amara laughed so hard she had to sit down.

The guide, Mr. Finn, arrived with a puzzled face. The announcement should have said magnificent storm. He turned off the exhibit and called the technician. She could come that afternoon. Meanwhile, three families were waiting to see the ship.

Amara asked whether they could tell the ship’s story themselves. Mr. Finn liked the idea, but reminded them that visitors needed a clear path and the glass case must not be touched. He brought paper, cardboard, and a book about the ship.

Leo wanted crashing waves and a giant sea monster. The book described a cargo ship that carried wool and tea. It had survived a storm, but there was no sea monster. “We can save that for a made-up story,” Amara said.

They divided the real story into three parts: the ship leaving port, the storm, and its return. Mr. Finn checked their notes. Leo made wave sounds by rubbing two sheets of paper together. Amara tested a cardboard thunder sheet.

Her first thunderclap was enormous. A toddler covered his ears. Amara stopped at once. They tried a softer version and warned visitors before each sound. A small sign explained that the paper storm was a live replacement for the broken exhibit.

At their first performance, Leo forgot the name of the port. Amara pointed to the notes. He found his place and continued. A child in the front row offered a very convincing seagull call. Mr. Finn invited one gentle call at the beginning.

By the third show, the storm had waves, rain, a gull, and two narrators who no longer rushed. When the ship reached home, the audience tapped their knees for the sound of the harbor bell. Nobody mentioned the missing projector.

The technician arrived and found two problems: a loose cable and a test recording accidentally selected during an update. The squeak had been a sound check. She repaired the cable, chose the correct recording, and ran the exhibit twice.

Leo expected their paper storm to be packed away. Instead, Mr. Finn asked whether they would perform once more before the last projected show. “Visitors have enjoyed hearing you tell it,” he said. Amara carefully flattened their rumpled notes.

At closing time, Amara chose a postcard of the ship. On the back she wrote, I saw a storm made from paper. Leo added a tiny sea monster in the corner. “That part is fiction,” he told her. “Obviously,” she replied. “It is wearing boots.”

title: Captain Ink and the Missing Island
description: Captain Ink was an octopus with excellent maps and terrible handwriting.
pages: Captain Ink was an octopus with excellent maps and terrible handwriting. His crew could read his charts only after turning them upside down, sideways, and occasionally backward. Today, the captain had promised a picnic on Button Island. He had drawn a very clear sandwich beside it.

The crew sailed to the marked spot. There was water, more water, and a gull sitting on a buoy. There was no island. First Mate Pearl, a young seal, checked the chart. “Perhaps,” she said carefully, “this is another handwriting problem.”

Captain Ink compared the buoy’s number with the chart. It matched. A distant lighthouse stood in the right direction too. They were in the correct place. The captain stared over the rail. “Then someone has stolen our picnic island.”

Pearl did not think an island would fit in a thief’s pocket. She suggested asking the lighthouse keeper by radio. The keeper laughed kindly. “Button Island is a sandbar. Check the tide table.” Captain Ink found the table under a biscuit tin.

At high tide, the sandbar was covered. At low tide, it appeared again. Their last visit had been at low tide. The captain had drawn the island but forgotten to note when it could be seen. He crossed out STOLEN in his log.

Low tide was several hours away. The crew could not simply wait in the shallow channel, where the falling water might leave their boat stuck. The lighthouse keeper directed them to a safe harbor. They followed the marked route and tied up there.

At the harbor, Pearl opened the picnic basket. The bread was dry, but the captain had packed eight spoons and no knife. “Eight arms,” he explained. Pearl used the café’s picnic table, and the café owner lent them what they needed.

They made sandwiches while Captain Ink corrected the chart. He added the words VISIBLE AT LOW TIDE in large letters. Then he drew a clock. Pearl asked him to include the date of the tide table, since the times changed.

Later, they watched from the harbor as a pale strip slowly appeared on the water. Gulls landed first. Soon Button Island looked exactly like the captain’s drawing, except for the enormous sandwich symbol. The crew cheered its return.

They decided to keep their picnic at the harbor. The little sandbar had no shade, and the tide would eventually cover it again. A safe viewpoint was enough. Captain Ink sketched the changing shape while Pearl counted gulls.

On the way home, the captain announced a new rule: every chart would be checked by another crew member. Pearl agreed, provided they also checked the picnic basket. She held up the eight spoons. The captain looked mildly offended.

That evening, he labeled the spoons with numbers so none would be lost. His handwriting was still terrible, but Pearl could read one through eight. Beneath the chart of Button Island, she added a small drawing of the harbor picnic table. It was much easier to find.

title: The Bake-Off Disaster
description: Aisha and her cousin Tom entered the junior bake-off with a plan for a three-layer berry cake.
pages: Aisha and her cousin Tom entered the junior bake-off with a plan for a three-layer berry cake. Their aunt would handle the oven. They would measure, mix, decorate, and make all important artistic decisions. Tom’s first decision was that the cake needed a tower.

Aisha preferred a neat cake with berries around the edge. They sketched both designs. The tower looked exciting, so they agreed to try it. Their aunt asked them to check the rules. Every part had to be edible, and they had one large tray.

The cake layers cooled on racks. Tom spread cream between them. Aisha added berries. The tower stood upright for three wonderful seconds. Then the top layer slid to the left. Tom caught it with a clean plate before it hit the table.

They rebuilt it with more cream. This made the layers slide even faster. Aisha pressed her lips together. “More of the same thing is not helping.” Their aunt checked the cake: the middle was still a little warm, which was softening the filling.

They put the layers aside to cool completely. There was an hour left. Tom stared at their drawing. “We could use a stick through the middle.” Aisha pointed to the rules. They had no suitable edible support, and rushing a new structure seemed risky.

While waiting, they tasted a small broken piece with cream and berries. It was delicious. Aisha looked at the clear dessert cups in the cupboard. “Does the entry have to be one tall cake?” They read the rules again. It did not.

They called the organizer to check that small portions on one tray were allowed. Yes, as long as they listed the ingredients and served the required number of portions. Tom drew a new plan: a tiny landscape made of berry cups.

They cut the cooled cake into small pieces and layered them in the cups with cream and fruit. Aisha made a hill of berries in each one. Tom arranged mint leaves like trees. Their aunt helped keep the cold ingredients chilled until judging.

The tray looked like a row of little gardens. Tom wanted to call it The Tower That Fell Over. Aisha worried that sounded like a failure. “It is what happened,” Tom said. They shortened the name to Fallen Tower Berry Cups.

At the bake-off, another team had built a perfect chocolate castle. Aisha felt a small pinch of envy. Then a judge tasted a berry cup and asked about the name. Tom told the story, including their unsuccessful extra-cream repair.

They won a ribbon for best use of fruit, not for the tallest cake. On the ride home, Aisha held the ribbon while Tom balanced the empty tray. “The castle was amazing,” she said. Tom agreed. He had drawn its towers in his notebook.

The next weekend, they tried a smaller cake tower with fully cooled layers and a sturdier plan. It stayed up. They ate it at the kitchen table. Aisha still requested a berry cup on the side. Some accidents, she had decided, were worth making again on purpose.

title: The Last Stop on Platform Three
description: Mara’s grandfather collected railway tickets.
pages: Mara’s grandfather collected railway tickets. He kept them in biscuit tins, which meant visiting children were often disappointed. One rainy afternoon, Mara found a ticket marked Platform Three—Last Service. The station in their town had only two platforms. “Then where,” she asked, “did this train go?”

Grandfather remembered a branch line that closed before Mara was born. It ran to a hilltop village called Bellweather. He had traveled on its final train as a boy. His strongest memory was not the engine or the crowd. It was someone carrying an enormous blue door.

Mara told her friend Dev, who immediately imagined a secret room. Grandfather warned that memory was not a photograph. The door might have been green. The next Saturday, he took them to meet the railway historian, Mrs. Shaw, at the station office.

Mrs. Shaw unfolded an old plan. Platform Three had stood behind the present bicycle shelter. The branch line’s last carriage had carried passengers, parcels, and items from the closing station. A newspaper photograph showed a door leaning against a luggage cart. It looked dark, but the photograph was black and white.

A label on the cart read READING ROOM. Dev announced that the door must have led to a secret railway library. Mrs. Shaw found a list of station furniture: benches, a clock, bookshelves, and one door. The items had been given to the Bellweather village hall.

They arranged a visit with the hall’s caretaker. The old railway track was now a walking path, but they traveled by bus because rain was forecast. At the hall, Mara saw modern glass doors. None looked remotely like the one in the photograph.

The caretaker remembered renovations several years earlier. An old door had been removed from a cupboard and stored in the attic. He brought it downstairs while the children waited. Under scratches and a coat of gray paint, a strip of blue showed near the hinge.

On the door’s inside surface were pencil marks: short lines with dates and names. Mara thought they were measurements. Dev suggested a coded timetable. The caretaker smiled. “Children’s heights,” he said. “The hall used to hold an after-school reading group.”

One name near the bottom was Grandfather’s. He stared, then laughed. He had forgotten joining the reading group after his family moved to Bellweather. The door had traveled on the last train, just as he remembered, but its story had continued long after the railway closed.

Mara wanted the door displayed at the station immediately. The caretaker hesitated. Several local families had names on it. It was part of the hall’s history too. Grandfather suggested making a photograph of the marks and inviting those families to share what they remembered.

At the spring exhibition, the door stood on a secure display frame in the village hall. Beside it were the train ticket, the newspaper photograph, and a map of the branch line. Visitors added memories on separate cards so the original marks stayed untouched.

Dev admitted that the secret-library theory had been more exciting at first. Then an elderly visitor found her childhood height beside Grandfather’s and challenged him to measure again. Mara borrowed a tape measure. For the next ten minutes, the railway exhibition became an extremely competitive height contest.

title: The Clockwork Whale
description: Every hour, the clockwork whale in the aquarium lobby opened its mouth and released a cloud of wooden fish.
pages: Every hour, the clockwork whale in the aquarium lobby opened its mouth and released a cloud of wooden fish. The fish swung from fine wires, circling before folding back inside. Jun had watched it since he was small. This year, his grandfather was repairing it, and he was finally allowed to help.

The whale had stopped halfway through its noon performance. Its mouth hung open, and one fish dangled upside down. Grandfather disconnected the mechanism before opening the side panel. Inside lay wheels, levers, and a tangle of motion Jun could not begin to follow.

Jun wanted to turn the largest wheel. Grandfather asked him to sketch the parts first. Each line on his drawing represented a connection. When he traced the wire from the upside-down fish, he found a bent guide ring. It was catching the wire whenever the whale opened its jaw.

The ring was easy to replace. The next problem was not. A small toothed wheel had lost a tooth, and the maker no longer sold that part. Grandfather could have a replacement made, but it would take a week. The aquarium’s anniversary celebration was in three days.

Jun suggested removing the fish that depended on the broken wheel. Grandfather explained that several movements shared the same mechanism. Removing one part without understanding the others might damage more. Jun crossed out his quick fix. His sketch was beginning to look like a spiderweb after a storm.

At home, he built a cardboard model with paper fasteners. It did not move like the real whale, but pulling one strip opened its mouth. His younger sister made paper fish and held them behind it. When the mouth opened, she fanned them outward and shouted, “Lunch!”

Jun laughed, then stopped. The real whale could wait for its proper repair. Perhaps visitors could still see how the idea worked. He brought the model to Grandfather, who suggested asking the aquarium educators whether they wanted a hands-on display for the anniversary.

The educators liked it, but Jun’s first model tore after six children used it. He had built it for one careful person, himself. They reinforced the moving strips, rounded sharp corners, and added a handle that was easy to grip. His sister tested it with great enthusiasm.

For the celebration, the silent clockwork whale remained behind a barrier with a short explanation of the repair. Beside it, Jun’s cardboard whale opened and closed all afternoon. Visitors took turns moving the handle while Grandfather showed them a large diagram of the original mechanism.

One boy asked why the real whale could not simply be replaced with the cardboard one. Jun considered this. His model showed the main movement, but not the many timed motions, the careful balance, or the fish folding away. A useful model, he explained, did not do everything the original did.

A week later, the new wheel arrived. Grandfather fitted it and tested the whale before reopening the display. Jun watched the fish turn smoothly through the air. For the first time, he could picture the hidden sequence that made the performance happen.

The aquarium kept his cardboard whale at the activity table. His sister demanded a small sign crediting her fish. Jun made one. Then she requested a cardboard shark, three times larger, with working teeth. Grandfather handed them a fresh sheet of paper. “Start,” she said, “with a drawing.”

title: The Secret of the Silent Theater
description: The old Lantern Theater had been silent for years.
pages: The old Lantern Theater had been silent for years. When the town announced a weekend tour, Priya persuaded her friends Ben and Tess to come. Ben expected ghosts. Tess expected dust. Priya hoped to find the painted moon her mother remembered from childhood plays.

Mr. Lyle, the caretaker, led them past rows of folded seats. The stage smelled of wood and old curtains. At the back stood painted scenery: a forest, a castle wall, and a moon taller than Priya. Its smiling face had one crooked eyebrow.

As Mr. Lyle spoke, a faint tapping came from behind the moon. Ben grabbed Tess’s sleeve. Three taps, a pause, then two. The caretaker stopped talking. The sound stopped too. “Probably the building settling,” he said, but he did not sound completely certain.

They stayed with him while he checked behind the scenery. Nothing moved. No animal appeared. A narrow metal pipe ran up the wall, and an old speaking tube ended near the floor. Long ago, stage workers had used it to send messages between rooms.

Tess asked whether another end might be open. Mr. Lyle checked a maintenance plan. The tube connected to the former ticket office, where volunteers were sorting posters. One volunteer had been tapping a pencil against a box resting on the tube’s metal rim.

Mystery solved, Ben declared, sounding disappointed. But Priya had noticed something else: small painted stars on the back of the moon, invisible to the audience. Beside them was a sentence: For Elsie, who always wanted the best view. No surname, no date.

Mr. Lyle found programs in the theater archive. Several listed an Elsie Hart as a scenery painter. Priya wondered whether the message was for her. A later program listed another Elsie, a child performer. The name alone was not enough to choose between them.

They asked permission to photograph the message for the town history group. A week later, a reply arrived from Elsie Hart’s daughter. Her mother had painted the stars for her own little sister, also named Elsie, who used to watch rehearsals from backstage.

The younger Elsie had been too shy to join the performances. From behind the moon, she could hear the music without facing the audience. Her sister painted a private sky where she waited. Priya imagined the small girl sitting under stars nobody else could see.

For the theater’s reopening fundraiser, the organizers planned to repaint the scenery. Priya showed them the reply and the photographs. A conservator recommended preserving the original moon and making a new copy for performances. The hidden stars would be displayed with their story.

At the fundraiser, Ben helped operate a harmless tapping effect for a mystery sketch. Tess kept a checklist so no one mistook it for a real problem. Priya guided visitors to both sides of the old moon. The back drew just as much attention as the smiling face.

Her mother recognized the crooked eyebrow at once. She had never known about the stars. “I thought I knew that moon,” she said. Priya turned it gently on its display stand, with the caretaker’s help. “You knew the part that faced you.” Behind them, Ben’s carefully scheduled ghost began tapping.

title: The Great Playground Election
description: When the school received money to improve one corner of the playground, Eli immediately imagined a climbing wall.
pages: When the school received money to improve one corner of the playground, Eli immediately imagined a climbing wall. His friend Noor wanted a quiet garden. Finn wanted a slide shaped like a dragon. The principal said the student council could recommend a plan after consulting the school.

Eli volunteered to run a survey. He drew three enormous pictures and placed a voting jar beneath each one. At lunchtime, students dropped a counter into their favorite jar. The dragon slide won by a landslide. Finn began practicing a victory speech that included roaring.

Then the principal asked two questions: had every class participated, and did each person vote only once? Eli checked his notes. Younger classes had eaten lunch earlier. Several students had returned for extra counters because they liked the dragon picture. His results were not as clear as they looked.

Noor suggested a second survey during class time, with one response per student. Finn accused her of wanting another vote because her garden had lost. She admitted she was disappointed. “But the missing classes would still be missing if the garden had won,” she said.

They asked the office to help distribute the survey. This time, the pictures were the same size, and each choice had a short description. The descriptions mentioned who could use it, how much space it needed, and what upkeep it would require.

Before collecting answers, they learned that a full dragon slide cost more than the entire budget. Finn went quiet. The council could not fairly promise something the school could not afford. He redrew his idea as a low dragon-shaped climbing feature, with a route around it.

The results were close: climbing equipment first, garden second, dragon feature third. Noor asked students why they had chosen each option. Some wanted active play. Others wanted shade or a place to talk away from noise. Several liked the dragon mainly because it looked funny.

The council walked through the proposed area with a teacher and the groundskeeper. A large tree already provided shade near the fence. The groundskeeper suggested benches there, while a smaller climbing feature could fit nearby. They needed real quotes before knowing whether both were possible.

Eli feared that combining ideas would make everyone’s first choice smaller. Noor said that might be true, but the shared plan could serve more needs. Finn proposed painting the benches like a long dragon, so the tail curled toward the climbing area.

They compared costs and presented two affordable plans, explaining what each included and left out. Classes discussed them before the final vote. The combined plan won. Eli still wished for a taller wall, but he could explain why others preferred the shared space.

On opening day, the dragon bench had a green head, yellow scales, and an extremely lopsided smile. Noor read beneath the tree while Eli tried the climbing feature. Finn sat on the dragon’s nose and announced that his creature had finally entered public service.

For the council report, Eli included both surveys and explained the first one’s weaknesses. He kept one of the original voting jars on his desk. It now held pencils. When Finn suggested putting a victory label on it, Eli chose a different label: CHECK WHO IS MISSING.

title: A Dragon in the Weather Station
description: The hilltop weather station hired no dragons.
pages: The hilltop weather station hired no dragons. This was written nowhere, but Dr. Rao felt it should have been obvious. Nevertheless, a copper-colored dragon arrived on Tuesday carrying an application made from a cereal box. Its name was Ember. Its special skill, it said, was making warm air.

Dr. Rao’s children, Leena and Ash, were helping organize old weather charts during the school holiday. They wanted Ember to stay. Their mother agreed to a supervised trial, provided the dragon kept away from measuring equipment and produced no flames. Ember saluted with one wing.

For the first hour, everything went well. Ember carried empty folders and dusted a shelf with its tail. Then Ash noticed a strange reading: the outdoor temperature had jumped sharply, while the station down the hill reported no such change. Outside, the air did not feel unusually warm.

Leena checked the time of the jump. It matched Ember’s tea break. The dragon had rested beside the instrument shelter and breathed happily through its nose. No flames, just warm breath. Ember looked horrified. “I was following the rule exactly.”

Dr. Rao explained that a rule could miss a problem. The shelter needed air that had not been warmed by a nearby visitor, even a polite one. She marked the affected readings as unreliable rather than pretending they represented the weather. Ember moved its tea break to the far end of the yard.

Later, a delivery brought a windsock for the station’s public display. The old one had torn. Ember offered to hang it, but the staff used their normal equipment instead. The dragon watched while Leena checked that visitors would be able to see it from the path.

When the new windsock barely moved, Ember gave a helpful puff. It streamed straight out. Ash clapped, then stopped. The display now suggested a strong wind that did not exist. Ember lowered its head. “I keep making the weather more interesting.”

Leena had an idea. Their science-day exhibit needed a way to demonstrate moving air indoors. An artificial breeze would be useful there, as long as everyone knew its source. Dr. Rao approved a separate demonstration area with no measuring instruments nearby.

Ember practiced gentle puffs that moved paper streamers without scattering the notes. Too hard, and the streamers snapped sideways. Too softly, and nothing happened. Ash held a sign naming each trial while Leena recorded which distance worked best.

At science day, visitors compared the real outdoor windsock with streamers moved by Ember indoors. The signs explained the difference. One child asked whether all the station’s wind came from dragons. Ember firmly denied this, then sneezed into a large handkerchief.

The demonstration was a success, but Dr. Rao did not offer Ember a measuring job. Instead, the station invited it back as an education helper. Ember considered the title, then added it to the cereal-box application in copper ink. It was longer than weather dragon, but sounded official.

Before leaving, Ember checked the yard for instruments and chose a safe, distant spot for its tea. Leena brought biscuits. The windsock turned in a real breeze while the dragon held its breath around the cup. “You may breathe normally here,” Dr. Rao called. Ember looked enormously relieved.

title: The Island That Moved
description: When Bea was seven, she buried a tin of treasures on a tiny island in Lake Wren.
pages: When Bea was seven, she buried a tin of treasures on a tiny island in Lake Wren. The treasures were ordinary: a marble, a badge, a drawing of a dragon with six legs. At eleven, she wanted them back. Her brother Sam mainly wanted proof that the six-legged dragon had existed.

Their aunt, a lake scientist, agreed to take them out during a routine survey. Bea described the island beside a crooked pine. Aunt Ruth frowned. The island in that part of the lake had shifted after recent storms. “Shifted?” Sam said. “Islands do not usually get up and leave.”

This one was a floating mat of reeds, roots, and collected plant material. It looked solid from a distance, but Aunt Ruth would not let them step onto it. They would observe from the boat. Bea’s memory of standing there years earlier worried her aunt, who had not been on that childhood picnic.

At the old location, there was open water. Farther along the shore, a thick patch of reeds curved around a fallen branch. Bea recognized its shape—or thought she did. Sam pointed out that several reed patches looked like untidy green slippers. They needed something more definite than a familiar-looking curve.

Bea had brought a photograph from the picnic. In it, her younger self held the tin beside a wooden marker with a painted blue triangle. The marker had belonged to an earlier survey. Aunt Ruth found its number in a field notebook. That gave them a specific feature to search for.

They circled the nearest reed patch at a safe distance. No blue triangle. The second patch had a stake, but its paint was white. Then Sam spotted a sliver of blue near the third patch’s far edge, almost hidden by bent reeds. Aunt Ruth used binoculars to read the faded number.

It matched. Bea cheered, then remembered the tin. It might have sunk, rusted, or traveled elsewhere inside the moving mat. Aunt Ruth would not disturb a nesting area to retrieve it. She marked the position and explained that a later maintenance visit might allow staff to check safely.

Bea tried to hide her disappointment. Sam did not help by listing all the unpleasant things that might now live inside a rusty tin. On the way back, however, he quietly handed her the photograph. “At least the dragon is partly visible,” he said. One ridiculous leg stuck out above the lid.

Two weeks later, Aunt Ruth called. The mat had drifted near a maintained access point, away from the nesting birds. During scheduled work, the crew had found a small tin lodged among old roots beside the marker. Its lid was stuck. They had left it closed for Bea.

At the laboratory, the tin looked less like buried treasure than a very old sandwich box. Aunt Ruth opened it carefully. The marble survived. The badge was rusty. The drawing had become a pale blur, with a purple streak where the dragon’s wings had been. Bea felt unexpectedly close to tears.

Sam, who had prepared three jokes, said none of them. He placed the marble on a clean cloth and asked whether the picnic photograph could be enlarged. A technician showed them how a higher-resolution scan might reveal more of the drawing, though it could not recover details the photograph had never captured.

The enlarged picture showed four legs clearly and a suspicious green line that might have been a fifth. Bea could remember the sixth, but could not prove it. Sam finally grinned. “We have discovered the five-and-a-possible-six-legged dragon.” Bea laughed hard enough to fog the computer screen.

They made a new treasure display at home: the marble, the rusty badge, the blurred paper, and two drawings. Bea drew the dragon as she remembered it. Sam drew it as the photograph supported. They labeled both, and neither drawing went back into the lake.

For Aunt Ruth’s survey report, Bea wrote about recognizing the painted marker rather than trusting the island’s outline. For herself, she kept the old tin on her shelf. It was no longer a container for hidden treasure. It was a very good place to keep pencils, including the green one Sam refused to return.

title: The Midnight Radio Club
description: The Midnight Radio Club met at seven in the evening.
pages: The Midnight Radio Club met at seven in the evening. This disappointed its founder, Cass, but the community center closed at nine, and her father insisted that names did not override bedtime. The club had three members, a donated receiver, and a notebook full of stations they had managed to hear.

Omar preferred music. Jules preferred weather reports because they sounded reassuringly precise. Cass wanted a mystery. On Thursday, she got one: beneath a wash of static, a voice repeated, “The lantern is missing. Meet at the old bridge.” Then came four musical notes and silence.

Cass wrote the sentence down before anyone could argue about it. Jules thought the voice had said landing, not lantern. Omar was sure the final place was ridge, not bridge. They listened again, but the signal had faded. Cass’s father reminded them that a poor signal could make ordinary words sound strange.

They did not go searching for a bridge. Instead, they noted the time and receiver settings, then asked the center’s radio volunteer, Ms. Chen, to help. She explained that the receiver could pick up local broadcasts and that a nearby event might use a temporary low-power station.

The town’s night market was preparing to open on Saturday. Its organizers had permission to broadcast announcements and performances over a small area. Ms. Chen found the published frequency. It matched the club’s notes. Cass looked disappointed. A market announcement sounded much less mysterious than a missing lantern.

At the next meeting, they heard the sentence again, clearly this time: “The lantern is missing. Meet at the old bridge.” Cass sat upright. Omar recognized the four notes that followed. They belonged to a tune the school orchestra had rehearsed for the market’s storytelling show.

They contacted the organizer using the number on the public event page. She explained that the broadcast was a rehearsal of a radio play. The missing lantern was part of a fictional treasure hunt. The old bridge existed only in the script. Jules drew a large box around the word FICTION in their notebook.

Cass should have felt foolish, but the organizer had another problem. The recording of the play’s ending was damaged, and two performers were unavailable. Could the club help record replacement lines at the center’s supervised studio? Cass agreed before remembering to ask her father. Fortunately, he was already smiling.

The script followed a lighthouse keeper whose lantern vanished just before a festival. Cass played an apprentice, Omar a boat builder, and Jules a messenger who had one important line and wanted to deliver it flawlessly. Ms. Chen taught them to leave a pause before speaking and keep the paper away from the microphone.

Their first take included a chair squeak, a dropped pencil, and Cass saying “old fridge” instead of “old bridge.” Omar laughed through his next line. On the second take, Jules spoke so softly that the messenger seemed to be reporting from another county. They listened back and tried again.

By the fourth take, the scene worked. The lantern had not been stolen; the keeper had lent it to guide a late-arriving boat and forgotten to tell the apprentice. Cass thought the explanation needed a little more drama. The script already had fog, a bell, and a nearly missed festival, Ms. Chen pointed out.

On Saturday, families listened at the market while the school orchestra played the four-note theme. The club stood beside Cass’s father, waiting for their scene. When Jules’s line arrived, every word was clear. Omar squeezed his fist in triumph without making a sound.

A younger child asked whether the lantern was really missing. Cass explained that it was a play. She showed him the program, which named the performers and described the story. Then she told him how the club had mistaken the rehearsal for a real mystery. He found that almost as entertaining.

At eight forty-five, the Midnight Radio Club packed its equipment. Cass added a new page to the notebook: things to check before declaring a mystery. Omar added things that make excellent sound effects. Jules wrote the closing announcement, and this time nobody disagreed about a single word.

title: The Museum of Almost True Things
description: Theo’s class was making a museum in the school hall.
pages: Theo’s class was making a museum in the school hall. Each team had to display an object and explain its history. Most students chose something sensible: a family recipe card, an old camera, a football medal. Theo brought a giant feather and announced that it belonged to a dragon.

His partner, Iris, stared at him. The feather had come from a costume box. “Dragons are not the assignment,” she said. Theo argued that a dragon would attract more visitors than a recipe card. Their teacher, Mr. Ellis, agreed that presentation mattered, but evidence mattered too.

Theo proposed a compromise: an exhibit called Almost True Things. It would show how a dramatic label could change what visitors believed about an ordinary object. Mr. Ellis approved only if the explanation was clear and nobody left thinking the invented histories were real. Iris insisted on a reveal panel beside each object.

They selected three items: the feather, a tiny decorated shoe, and a dented metal cup. Theo wrote extravagant first labels. The feather came from a mountain dragon; the shoe belonged to a royal mouse; the cup had survived a journey to the center of the earth. Iris collected the actual histories.

The shoe was a souvenir from a doll festival. The cup had been used by the school’s old camping club. The feather was a painted costume prop made from synthetic material. Iris found the club’s photograph album, the shoe’s packaging, and a costume inventory. Theo admitted that the evidence display looked unexpectedly interesting.

During a practice visit, Theo placed the dramatic labels at eye level and the reveal panels underneath. His friend Milo read the dragon label, gasped, and ran to tell someone else before opening the panel. Iris folded her arms. Their exhibit had just done exactly what Mr. Ellis had warned against.

Theo argued that Milo should have read everything. Iris asked why they had made the exciting claim easiest to see and the correction harder to find. She was not accusing him of being cruel. That somehow made the question more uncomfortable. The design itself was encouraging the wrong conclusion.

They changed the heading to Three Invented Stories, Three Real Objects. Each object had two equally visible cards: Imagined History and What the Evidence Shows. Visitors could enjoy Theo’s inventions without needing to discover that they were inventions. Mr. Ellis approved the new arrangement.

Then Iris found a genuine puzzle. The camping photograph showed the same dent in the cup, but the caption named a year before the club was officially founded. Had the cup belonged to an earlier group? Had someone written the date incorrectly? This time, Theo resisted inventing an instant answer.

They asked the retired teacher who had donated the album. She remembered a small hiking group that later became the official camping club. However, she was unsure of the photograph’s exact year. The students recorded her explanation as a recollection and kept the uncertain date marked as uncertain.

On exhibition day, the dragon feather attracted plenty of attention. Visitors laughed at the royal mouse’s shoe, then lingered over the cup’s two possible dates. One parent remembered joining the early hiking group and offered to look for an old permission slip at home.

Theo began asking visitors what would help settle the date instead of telling them a dramatic answer. Someone suggested checking a newspaper report; another suggested comparing the students’ ages in the photograph. Iris added these possibilities to a research list, clearly separated from findings.

The museum closed before they solved the date completely. Their final card explained what they knew, what they suspected, and what they still wanted to check. Theo kept the imaginary underground journey on its own labeled card. It remained an excellent story, even beside the less tidy truth.

At the end of term, Mr. Ellis asked which object they would keep. Iris chose the cup. Theo chose the feather, then changed his mind. “The cup has an unfinished mystery,” he said. Iris handed him both. The dragon, apparently, could wait until the evidence came in.

title: The Race Nobody Finished
description: The Pine Street Cart Race had one rule everyone remembered: no motors.
pages: The Pine Street Cart Race had one rule everyone remembered: no motors. It had twelve other rules that most teams remembered only after being reminded. Jo and her cousin Malik had spent three weekends building a wooden cart with a bright orange nose. They called it Comet, although it moved more like a determined shopping trolley.

The course ran along a closed park path under adult supervision. One rider sat in each cart while teammates pushed on the flat stretches. Before the event, volunteers checked wheels, brakes, helmets, and the route. Jo wanted speed. Malik wanted every bolt checked twice. For once, their disagreements were useful.

Their main rivals were the Willow Team, whose cart was sleek, blue, and annoyingly quiet. Comet squeaked at every turn. Jo suspected the squeak cost them speed. Malik suspected it mainly cost them dignity. They tested both theories and found that the loose seat bracket, not the wheels, was making the noise.

By race morning, the squeak was fixed. Clouds gathered beyond the trees, but the forecast allowed time for the event before heavier rain. Organizers reminded everyone that conditions could change and the race would stop if necessary. Jo heard the warning, then immediately thought about the trophy.

Comet started well. Jo pushed while Malik steered, then they changed at the marked exchange zone. The Willow Team stayed just ahead. Near the small wooden bridge, Jo saw a blue wheel wobble. A moment later, the rival cart stopped crookedly at the edge of the path.

The marshal halted nearby carts and kept everyone clear. No one was hurt, but the Willow Team’s axle fastening had come loose. Their spare tool kit was back at the start. Malik held up Comet’s kit. Jo hesitated. Helping would not make their own cart any faster.

“The race is stopped anyway,” Malik said quietly. Jo handed the kit to the adult volunteer. Together, the teams waited while the fastening was checked. Then rain began, harder than predicted. Water streamed across the path toward the bridge, carrying leaves into a slippery pile.

The organizer canceled the remaining laps. Several teams groaned. One demanded that the current leader be declared the winner. Another argued that positions before the stoppage were unfair because some carts had already passed a narrow section and others had not. The rules did not cover this exact situation.

Jo wanted a result. They had worked too hard for nothing. Malik pointed to Comet, still whole and working, and to the repaired blue cart. “Not nothing,” he said. Jo knew he was right and found that deeply irritating. She was not ready to stop being disappointed.

Under the pavilion, the organizer explained that there would be no race winner that day. Times from an incomplete course could not fairly decide one. Instead, teams could demonstrate their designs once the rain eased, and the race would be rescheduled if a safe date could be found.

The Willow Team asked about Comet’s steering. Malik showed them the linkage while Jo described the seat-bracket squeak. Soon three teams were comparing repairs. The quiet blue cart had a clever wheel cover, but Comet’s steering was easier to adjust. Neither design was best at everything.

Jo still glanced at the unused trophy. She did not suddenly become pleased about the cancellation. But she began sketching a removable wheel cover on the back of their race number. One Willow teammate offered to send measurements. They exchanged notes before the families packed up.

A month later, the park could host the rescheduled event. Comet returned with smoother steering, a wheel cover, and a name painted more carefully on its nose. The Willow Team arrived with spare tools of their own. Jo shook their rider’s hand before climbing into the seat.

This time, Comet finished third. Jo would have preferred first. She accepted the small ribbon, then helped Malik wheel their cart toward the car. At the gate, the old seat bracket gave one unmistakable squeak. Malik bowed to the imaginary crowd. “Our signature sound,” he announced. Jo laughed before she could stop herself.

title: The Last Delivery to Mars
description: At fourteen, Ren was the youngest apprentice on the Mars greenhouse delivery team.
pages: At fourteen, Ren was the youngest apprentice on the Mars greenhouse delivery team. This mostly meant checking labels while other people did the exciting work. Her partner was a cargo robot named Patch, whose name described both its appearance and the repair history nobody wanted to discuss.

Their final delivery before a dust-storm shutdown was a small metal case for Greenhouse Seven. The manifest called it environmental equipment. Ren imagined a new sensor, perhaps a device important enough to earn her a place in the control room. Patch scanned the case and said, “Weight: disappointingly ordinary.”

The covered service route would close in forty minutes. Ren checked the approved path, their cart’s charge, and the case’s temperature indicator. The indicator was green. The greenhouse manager confirmed that the case should arrive before shutdown if possible, but crew safety came first. They set out through the connected service tunnels.

At Junction C, a maintenance barrier blocked their usual route. A damaged seal was being replaced. Patch calculated an alternative through the supply depot. It was longer, but still inside the protected network. Ren contacted control and received clearance before changing course. Her first important decision felt mostly like paperwork.

The depot was crowded with storm supplies. A supervisor directed them to wait behind a moving loader. Ren watched the minutes disappear. Patch noticed the case’s green indicator flicker yellow. Its label showed a permitted temperature range, and the depot was warmer than the tunnel they had left.

Ren wanted to hurry through the gap beside the loader. Patch blocked the cart with one metal foot. The supervisor had told them to wait. Ren swallowed her complaint and asked whether the case could be moved to the cooler staging shelf while they waited. The supervisor cleared a safe path to it.

The indicator returned to green. Ren called Greenhouse Seven to report the delay and temperature warning. This time, the manager explained the contents: carefully stored seeds for a small crop trial. They were not urgently needed that evening, but repeated temperature changes could affect the trial. Ren stared at the very ordinary-looking case.

Control offered two options. They could continue to the greenhouse, with little time left before route closure, or leave the case in the depot’s approved cool storage and complete delivery after the storm. Ren disliked the second option. She had wanted to finish every item on her first independent manifest.

Patch displayed the remaining time, but did not choose for her. Ren checked with the greenhouse manager and the depot supervisor. Both confirmed that the storage conditions were suitable and the delivery could wait. She arranged a documented handover, including the brief yellow warning, rather than treating it as if nothing had happened.

They returned to base before the service route closed. Ren’s manifest had one item marked STORED—DELIVERY PENDING. She expected criticism. Her supervisor asked three questions: was the case secure, did the receiving staff know, and was the condition recorded? Ren answered yes each time. “Then the job is under control,” the supervisor said.

The storm lasted two days. During the delay, Ren read about the crop trial. Greenhouse Seven was testing a compact bean plant that might use space efficiently. The seeds were not magic, and the trial might fail. That made keeping the conditions consistent more important, not less: researchers needed to understand what caused the results.

After the routes reopened, Ren and Patch collected the case. The depot log showed stable storage temperatures. They delivered it to the greenhouse, where the manager let Ren help check the labels against the planting plan. Patch remained by the door, carefully avoiding a watering hose it distrusted.

Weeks later, the first leaves unfolded. Some seedlings grew faster than others. Ren visited on her break and found the manager recording those differences without declaring success too early. A small label beside the tray named the delivery team, including Patch. The robot requested a copy for its maintenance panel.

Ren kept the completed manifest, with its delay and handover still visible. She had not delivered a dramatic machine or beaten the storm by seconds. Jo opened her notebook. She wrote the time of each visit and drew the window. Ben suggested checking again on a cloudy day. They did. Without the warm sunlight, the sail stayed white all afternoon.

The paint had not changed. The light had changed the way it looked. Jo crossed out her first guess but kept it in her notebook. “A wrong guess can be useful,” she said, “if it leads to a good question.”

title: Jay’s Green Engine
description: Jay and Grandpa arrived early for their steam train ride.
pages: Jay and Grandpa arrived early for their steam train ride. A green engine waited beside the platform. A brass J shone on its side. “My letter!” Jay said. He counted the big wheels while the driver checked the engine.

A red flag fluttered beside the station. Jay pointed at it. “Does that mean we cannot go?” Grandpa shook his head. “That is the station flag. The driver watches the railway signals.” Farther down the track, a signal showed red.

They climbed into a passenger car and found their seats. The train stayed still. Then another train rolled past on the next track. After it had cleared the junction, the signal for their train changed to green.

The whistle blew, and the green engine began to move. Jay watched the wheels turn faster. The station flag still fluttered behind them. “Our signal is green,” he told Grandpa. “But my engine was green all along!”

title: The Night Train Window
description: Mina pressed her nose near the train window.
pages: Mina pressed her nose near the train window. Outside, the fields were almost black. Inside, a little lamp lit her table. She set her toy fox beside her cup. Suddenly, another fox appeared outside the window!

“Mom! A fox is keeping up with our train!” Mina said. Mom leaned closer. “Try moving your toy.” Mina lifted it. The outside fox rose too. She tipped it sideways. The other fox tipped at exactly the same time.

“It is a reflection,” Mom said. “The glass is sending some light back toward us.” Mina cupped her hands around her eyes to block the lamp’s light. Now she could see a farmhouse and three lights on a hill.

Mina sat back and held her fox toward the glass. “Meet your twin,” she whispered. When Mom lowered the lamp, the reflection grew faint. Mina tucked the fox into her bag. One fox was plenty for a night train trip.

title: The Mixed-Up Cargo
description: Leo and Aunt May watched a blue diesel engine at the freight depot.
pages: Leo and Aunt May watched a blue diesel engine at the freight depot. Two wagons waited for their cargo. One would carry apples to a market. The other would carry sunflowers to a garden shop. Workers pushed crates across the platform.

A worker stopped beside the apple wagon. He held a delivery list, then looked at the crates. Yellow petals poked through one crate. “These are not apples!” he called. Leo smiled. Even from behind the fence, he could see the flowers.

The workers checked both stacks. The crates had been put beside the wrong wagons. They moved the flowers to the garden-shop wagon and the apples to the market wagon. Then they checked the labels against the delivery list again.

At last, the wagon doors closed. The diesel engine pulled its load out of the depot. “The flowers nearly went shopping for apples,” Leo said. Aunt May laughed. “Good thing someone checked before they left.” Leo waved as the last wagon passed.

title: The Snake in the Leaves
description: Nora saw something pale beside a log in the school garden.
pages: Nora saw something pale beside a log in the school garden. It looked like a thin, empty sock. “Did someone lose this?” she asked. Her teacher, Ms. Bell, asked the class to stay on the path while she looked.

“It is a snake’s old skin,” Ms. Bell said. “Snakes shed their outer skin as they grow.” Ben peered at the leaves from the path. “Where is the snake?” Brown leaves covered the ground. At first, Nora saw nothing else.

Then a curved shape moved beside the log. A small brown snake slipped through the leaves. Its colors were so close to the leaves that Nora had missed it. Everyone watched quietly from the path and gave it room to move.

The snake disappeared under the log. Back in class, Nora drew brown leaves and hid a brown snake among them. Ben searched her picture. “Found it!” he said. Nora added the pale skin beside the log. This time, she knew what it was.

title: The Bell Beyond the Bridge
description: A little bell hung beside Fernwood Bridge.
pages: A little bell hung beside Fernwood Bridge. Visitors rang it so Rabbit could bring out the ferry when the footpath flooded. One windy morning, the bell rang again and again. Rabbit hurried down, but nobody was waiting. “Someone is playing a trick,” he grumbled.

Pip offered to watch from the oak tree. Soon a gust bent a nearby branch. Its twig struck the bell. Ding! Pip climbed down and showed Rabbit the branch. Rabbit looked embarrassed. He had blamed a visitor before checking the cause.

They tied the branch away from the bell with a soft strip of cloth. The ringing stopped. Rabbit returned to his breakfast, but Pip stayed to test their repair. He pulled the bell rope once. The sound was so faint that Rabbit did not hear it.

The cloth was touching the bell too. Pip moved the knot higher, leaving the bell free. This time Rabbit heard a clear ring and waved from his window. The repair now stopped the false alarms without stopping the real signal.

That afternoon, a squirrel rang for the ferry. Rabbit arrived with a basket of buns. “For my first actual passenger today,” he said. Pip took one for himself. Listening carefully had turned out to be hungry work.

title: The Passenger with the Notebook
description: A passenger boarded the green train carrying a thick notebook.
pages: A passenger boarded the green train carrying a thick notebook. At each stop she wrote something, frowned, and crossed it out. Jay thought she must be a railway inspector. He sat straighter and tried to keep his teddy from falling into the aisle.

When the train paused beside the sea, the passenger counted the gulls outside. Then she counted the windows. Jay whispered to the conductor, “Are we in trouble?” The conductor smiled. “Why do you think that?” Jay explained about the notebook and the frowns.

“You could ask her,” the conductor suggested. Jay waited until she put her pencil down. “Are you checking our train?” he asked. The passenger showed him a page filled with verses. She was writing a poem and searching for a word that rhymed with bay.

Jay suggested day. The passenger had tried that. He suggested sway, remembering how the carriage moved. Her face brightened. She wrote a line about watching sailboats sway while the little train rolled beside the bay.

At the last stop, she read her poem aloud. Teddy received a brief mention in the final verse. Jay had spent half the journey worrying about an inspection that existed only in his imagination. Next time, he decided, he would ask a question sooner.

title: The Shortest Letter
description: Bot sorted hundreds of letters at Moon Mail.
pages: Bot sorted hundreds of letters at Moon Mail. One envelope contained only two words: THANK YOU. There was no name beneath them. The address said POST OFFICE. Bot read it twice. “Two words,” he said. “Someone must have forgotten the rest.”

Zip disagreed. “Perhaps that is the whole message.” Bot thought letters should explain things. He put the note beside his scanner and worked through a difficult pile of parcels. One label was torn; another had two different addresses. By midday, his wheels felt unusually heavy.

Then Bot noticed the note again. He remembered helping a family receive a birthday package before their celebration. Perhaps the letter came from them. Or perhaps it came from the musician whose strings he had delivered. He could not be certain.

Bot placed the note on the staff board. Other workers paused to read it. Each remembered someone they had helped. Nobody could prove who had sent it, but everyone understood the feeling behind it. The little note seemed to make the busy room quieter.

At closing time, Bot wrote his own letter to the maintenance crew. It was longer than two words because he wanted to mention the repaired ramp. Still, he began with the same two. Short letters, he decided, could carry surprisingly large messages.

title: The Cake That Would Not Stand
description: Lila designed a cake shaped like a tall lighthouse.
pages: Lila designed a cake shaped like a tall lighthouse. She drew six layers and a tiny sugar lamp. Grandpa admired the drawing, then asked how the cake would stay upright. “It will stand because it looks wonderful,” Lila replied. Grandpa raised one eyebrow.

They built a small practice version from soft sponge cake. Before the fourth layer was added, it leaned sideways. Lila caught it with a plate. Her magnificent lighthouse now looked like a sleeping walrus. She was too disappointed to laugh, although Grandpa looked tempted.

Grandpa showed her how a wider base could support fewer, sturdier layers. Lila revised her drawing. She also made the lamp from paper and placed it beside the cake instead of on top. The new lighthouse was shorter, but it stayed straight.

During the party, a guest asked why a paper lamp stood beside the cake. Lila explained her tests. The guest said he designed real buildings and often changed plans after testing them. Lila looked proudly at her second drawing, complete with crossed-out lines.

Grandpa brought out the practice cake as extra slices. “Sleeping walrus, anyone?” he asked. This time Lila laughed first. Both designs had finally found a useful job, though only one had become a lighthouse.
